newsitem.title: UK: BA says American deal still on track.
newsitem.headline: BA says American deal still on track.

text.p: British Airways remained optimistic on Tuesday that its proposed alliance with American Airlines would take off this summer despite the threat of a clash with the European Commission.

"The deal...is planned to be implemented during the course of the early summer of this year and I see no reason why it should not be possible to achieve that timetable," chief executive Robert Ayling told BBC radio.

On Monday Commission sources said Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert had told Britain the Commission would not tolerate British approval of the deal if it conflicted with the Commission's own views. In a letter sent to British Trade Secretary Ian Lang's department, Van Miert said the Commission would defend its view in the European Court of Justice if necessary.
Asked about this apparent Commission challenge to British proposals to conditionally approve the deal, Ayling said: "I remain optimistic that we can get through this and get approval".

While Lang's Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) declined comment as it had not yet seen the letter and had not yet given its own final ruling on the deal, Ayling said it was too early to say that the regulators would end up in conflict.

In December Lang proposed conditions for allowing the alliance to go ahead, including a demand that the companies release a total of 168 weekly runway slots at London Heathrow airport to make room for more competition.
But an EU source said that 168 slots would not be enough to ensure adequate competition -- the Commission would want a figure nearer 300 to 400 and these slots would have to be surrendered, not sold.
Shares in British Airways shrugged off the Commission's warning on Tuesday, rising two pence to 602-1/2 pence.

But some investment analysts took a more cautious stance, advising investors that at best BA and American could face further delays in getting all the approvals needed on both sides of the Atlantic and that they might have to make concessions.
"I view the situation with a lot of caution. The hurdles are just so many and so political," said James Halstead, London-based airlines analyst with Credit Lyonnais.
"The trouble is that British Airways has always talked about this alliance as though it's a done deal," said another analyst, Nigel Davies of brokers Panmure Gordon.

"There is now a very big risk that BA will be left with a gap in its U.S. alliances this year," he said, referring to the fact that BA's divorce from its current transatlantic partner USAir is due to take effect from the end of March.
BA's opponents welcomed the news that the European Commission had lent its voice to critics of the deal.

British rival Virgin Atlantic Airways said the British proposals for approving the deal were entirely inadequate to enable other airlines to mount effective transatlantic competition to BA and American at Heathrow.

"Virgin warned the British Government in writing at the time the Office of Fair Trading was beginning to investigate this deal (last year) that unless the UK authorities did a proper and competent job...then there would be every excuse for the Commission to intervene," said Virgin's spokesman Will Whitehorn.

But Ayling said Van Miert's claims that the plan would substantially restrict competition on all routes between Britain and the United States were wrongly based, as the deal would only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree an "open skies" treaty to open their transatlantic market to free competition.
